sentences.text: DG32-2DOM is the attention variant of Deepgrid Semi's DG32-LITE motor-control chip.
It keeps the dual-core lockstep controller and adds an INT8 attention engine on its own clock, so a drive can watch its own motor for faults.
The design is complete and in physical trials.
Every figure here is a post-route, simulated or analytic value, and each one is labelled.
Here is the answer on one slide.
DG32-2DOM is DG32-LITE plus an attention engine, not a new core.
The lockstep CPU pair, boot path, peripherals and sixty-four-pin pinout are identical.
The engine runs at one hundred fourteen megahertz, its output is bit-exact to the software model, and one query row costs about thirty-two hundred cycles, by analysis.
Three findings forced the design.
The lockstep core tops out around fifty-five to sixty-two megahertz, so the control domain has to stay at fifty.
The engine is the throughput consumer, so it gets its own faster clock.
And adding its memory to the DG32-LITE floorplan made routing time out, so the variant gets a larger die of its own.
This is the architecture.
On the left, the fifty megahertz control domain: everything in DG32-LITE.
On the right, the one hundred fourteen megahertz compute domain: the attention engine and its key and value buffers.
Between them sit three clock-domain bridges.
The engine reaches memory only through those bridges, so it can never stall the control core.
None of the base chip is redesigned.
The safety pair and its fault latch, the boot ROM and memory, and every motor and sensing block come straight from DG32-LITE's own design files.
So the control loop still costs roughly three hundred hardware cycles, and because the engine needs no pins, the nine-by-nine millimetre package and its pinout stay put.
Only the clocking changes.
One kick computes a band of query rows of one attention head, end to end.
Firmware programs the shapes.
A shared multiply array computes Q times K transpose.
A row maximum indexes a table of softmax weights.
The engine forms the weighted sum, divides once per row, saturates the result to INT8, and writes the output back to memory.
Why not squeeze the engine down to four bits?
Because attention spreads its weight thin.
Across roughly four hundred keys that look alike, each key earns about a quarter of one percent, and four-bit arithmetic cannot represent that: every weight became zero, and so did the answer.
The engine instead carries weights at fifteen bits through a forty-bit sum, which holds exactly past a hundred thousand keys, and only narrows to INT8 at the very end.
An engine that streamed its data across the shared bus would spend its time fighting the CPU for it.
So its working data is loaded once per kick into memory right beside it, and each query row rereads what is already there.
That keeps one attention head near one percent of bus time; resending the data for each row would cost roughly four hundred times as much.
The DMA can even do the loading without involving the processor.
The usual way to join two clocks is a FIFO buffer.
This design skips it, because data crosses between the domains so seldom: inputs go over once, and results come back once.
A four-phase request and acknowledge, synchronised on arrival, is small and easy to prove safe.
Programming commands cross one after another, and a whole block of reads or writes travels as a single transfer.
The engine's cost can be worked out before silicon, because it is plain arithmetic.
At sixteen lanes and four hundred keys, with keys of thirty-two bytes and values of sixty-four, combining the values takes half of each row, about sixteen hundred cycles.
Scoring the keys takes a quarter, requantising about seven hundred, and the divide just forty-eight, roughly thirty-two hundred and forty in all.
A bench measurement replaces that estimate once first silicon arrives.
Splitting the clocks worked: both domains close timing after place-and-route, with positive slack.

The fifty megahertz control side has zero point three nanoseconds of slack, and the one hundred fourteen megahertz engine side zero point one nine, on a die of three point four by four point five millimetres.
Those are layout results, not silicon; the silicon numbers come with bring-up.
What is it for?
Catching a wearing bearing, or a drive that starts behaving oddly, without an extra processor on the board, because the motor controller watches its own motor.
The STM32G0 can only run that kind of model in software, so a hardware engine sets DG32-2DOM apart.
On the roadmap it runs alongside DG32-LITE's first silicon, with its design finished and undergoing physical trials.
So what should stay with you?
First, the safety controller was left alone; the engine was built around it, not into it.
Second, nothing is lost to rounding, and the hardware reproduces the reference software's output exactly.
Third, the price of each row is already known from analysis, at about thirty-two hundred cycles.
The next step is to measure all of it on real silicon.
